Monsters
MON-sturz
n. pl. (great creatures; in Lamentations 4:3, the sea monsters that nurse their young while Jerusalem's mothers do not)
From Latin monstrum, a portent or omen, from monere, to warn. At Lamentations 4:3 sea monsters renders Hebrew tannin, a great creature of the deep.

Biblical Definition

Jeremiah is measuring the famine in the besieged city by comparing his own people with animals, and the comparison goes against them: Even the sea monsters draw out the breast, they give suck to their young ones: the daughter of my people is become cruel, like the ostriches in the wilderness. The great creatures of the deep nurse their young. The ostrich, in Job's description, leaves her eggs in the earth and is hardened against her young ones as though they were not hers. And Jerusalem, says the prophet, has become the second and not the first. The next verse spells out what he means: The tongue of the sucking child cleaveth to the roof of his mouth for thirst: the young children ask bread, and no man breaketh it unto them.

The word in Hebrew is tannin, used across Scripture for great creatures — the ones God created on the fifth day and pronounced good, the serpent Aaron's rod became, the dragon of Isaiah's poetry, Leviathan in Job. The Bible has no category of independently evil beasts; every creature in it is God's, and the great ones are among the exhibits when He answers Job out of the whirlwind. Which is precisely what makes Lamentations 4:3 so terrible. The monsters behave as God made them to behave, and the covenant people, under the last extremity of a siege they were warned about for forty years, do not.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): unnatural productions; animals of huge or unusual size; in Scripture, great creatures of the sea.

expand to see more

MONSTER, n. An animal of unnatural form, or of extraordinary size; anything out of the common course of nature.

WHALE, n. The general name of an order of animals inhabiting the ocean, the largest of created animals.

OSTRICH, n. A fowl of the largest size, of the African deserts, remarkable for neglecting her eggs.

SUCK, v.t. To draw with the mouth; to draw milk from the breast.

CRUEL, a. Disposed to give pain to others; inhuman; hard-hearted; void of pity.

Key Scripture

Lamentations 4:3 — "Even the sea monsters draw out the breast, they give suck to their young ones: the daughter of my people is become cruel, like the ostriches in the wilderness."

Lamentations 4:4 — "The tongue of the sucking child cleaveth to the roof of his mouth for thirst: the young children ask bread, and no man breaketh it unto them."

Job 30:29 — "I am a brother to dragons, and a companion to owls."

Lamentations 2:11 — "Mine eyes do fail with tears, my bowels are troubled, my liver is poured upon the earth, for the destruction of the daughter of my people; because the children and the sucklings swoon in the streets of the city."

Modern Corruption

The great creatures of Scripture are made into mythology or into demons, when the Bible files them among God's works and uses them as a standard by which His people are judged.

expand to see more

Two readings misplace the tannin. One treats Leviathan, the dragon and the sea monsters as borrowed Near Eastern myth, the residue of a chaos-combat story that Israel outgrew. The other makes them straightforwardly demonic, so that every mention becomes a spiritual-warfare text. Genesis 1 forecloses both: God created great whales, and God saw that it was good. They appear again in Job 41 as the LORD's own exhibit of a creature no man can draw out with a hook, and again in Psalm 104 as one He formed to play in the sea. They are creatures, magnificent and untamable, and they belong to Him.

That is what gives Lamentations 4:3 its edge. Jeremiah is not invoking a monster to horrify; he is citing a well-known fact about animals, that even the great creatures of the deep feed their young, and setting it against what the siege had made of his own city. Scripture repeatedly uses the ordinary faithfulness of creatures to shame the covenant people — the ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib, but Israel doth not know; the stork in the heaven knoweth her appointed times. The animals keep their instincts. Men break covenants, and the prophets make the comparison deliberately.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tannin (H8577), a great creature, sea monster or dragon; ya'en (H3283), the ostrich; akzar (H393), cruel.

expand to see more

Hebrew tannin (H8577) — a sea monster, a great creature; created on the fifth day and called good.

Hebrew ya'en (H3283) — the ostrich; in Job hardened against her young as though they were not hers.

Hebrew akzar (H393) — cruel; what the daughter of the people had become.

Hebrew liwyathan (H3882) — Leviathan; the LORD's exhibit in Job 41.

Hebrew bath ammi (H1323, H5971) — the daughter of my people; Jeremiah's name for Jerusalem in the Lamentations.

Usage

"“Even the sea monsters draw out the breast” — an ordinary fact about animals, used to shame a city."

"“the daughter of my people is become cruel” — the verdict of the comparison."

"“the young children ask bread, and no man breaketh it unto them” — what it meant on the street."
